title: I Printed the Municipal Leaf-Drop Scale After They Zeroed With a Thumb

parts.text: I backed to bay five at 9:07 a.m. and attendant Voss was already zeroing the scale with a thumb on our numbered bags. The sign said: PAY BY WEIGHT. BAGS ON THE PLATE. NO HANDS. I was thirty-nine, resident, holding a coupon that listed our load. Voss shrugged. "Hands are rounding." I photographed the sign, the display, and his thumb on the plate. Then I asked for the scale log. At 9:15 public works pinged why Voss's name was on our zero. I kept my voice lot-quiet and let the timestamp talk. A sign is only a sign until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: Public works can see Voss's thumb on the plate during our weigh.

social.video_title: He zeroed the leaf-drop scale with a thumb — Part 1/2
social.description: Municipal bay, a thumb on the plate, a pay-by-weight sign he posted. I logged the zero. Would you have asked for the scale log?

parts.text: Voss called it a gust until public works asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the sign, and the thumb still. The plate went back to our bags. Voss ran the next load with two hands off and told the next attendant atmosphere was always about flow. Flow is a word attendants use when a sign exists. Scale policy now has a second line: HANDS ARE NOT ROUNDING. I keep our coupon on a labeled clip. Voss brown-bags his jokes. The bay finally looks like a weigh, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.description: Scale log, numbered bags, and a second line on the sign. Was a gust ever the plate?
